newsitem.title: USA: US T-bond outlook bleak, 7.25 pct yld seen - charts.
newsitem.headline: US T-bond outlook bleak, 7.25 pct yld seen - charts.

text.p: The technical outlook for the U.S. Treasury market deteriorated dramatically over the last few days, prompting chart analysts to forecast a near-term rise in the 30-year bond yield to 7.25 percent.

A recent selloff tied to stronger-than-expected fresh economic data has sent the market into a tailspin, boosting the yield on the benchmark bond up to 7.13 percent, the highest in almost seven weeks, from 7.04 at Thursday's close.
"(The outlook) is deteriorating. Technically there is very little to get excited about right now," said Walter Burke, senior technical analyst at consultant MCM MoneyWatch Inc.

"The reason is because the market continues to close on its lows. It closed on its lows yesterday, and it closed on its lows the day before. That is preventing it from getting any bottoming pattern," Burke added.
Chartists said they will be closely scrutinizing the market at Friday's close. If the bond yield finishes at or above 7.10 percent, it could indicate fresh selling next week, they said.
The 6-3/4 percent benchmark bond was quoted down 1-3/32 at 95-9/32 in early midday trade, yielding 7.13 percent.

"Closing through 7.10 (percent) increases the odds that the market will re-test the low of the year at 7.25 (percent)," said Michael Krauss, managing director and chief technical strategist at Chase Securities Inc.
Pundits said the long-term outlook for the market appears to be even gloomier at this point. "My longer-term target is still in the vicinity of 7.32 and 7.50 percent," Chase's Krauss added.
Analysts said the market broke several support levels over the last few sessions, which confirmed a shift to a more bearish trend.
"There is nothing special to think the market is going to bounce right here. We're taking out uptrend lines, we're taking out support levels," MCM's Burke said.

The new broad range for the bond market yield is now seen between 7.00 and 7.25 percent, with the area between 7.10 and 7.15 percent being the very short-term place where the market is likely to trade.
"The old lows, or the old yield highs, are now seen as the next support of significance," said a money market trader at a U.S. investment bank.

The U.S. bellwether yield touched its highest level of the year at 7.25 percent in intra-day trading on July 8. The highest closing level for the cash market so far this year was on June 12 at 7.20 percent, analysts said.
"I think that if we are to get there (to the 7.25 percent yield on the bond) it will be over the next week or so," MCM's Burke said.
The tone in the Treasury market turned bearish as a slew of fresh economic data suggested the economy was not slowing as much and as fast as many economists had previously thought.
A much stronger-than-expected Chicagoland Business Barometer for August was the spark that started the latest fire in the market.
The index, released on Friday, rose to a stunning 60.0 versus 51.2 in July. That reading was the highest since a 62.6 registered in February 1995.
A 1.8 percent rise in July factory orders reported Friday also weighed on prices and worsened the technical outlook, analysts said.
